session title: KEYNOTE:  The 200GW Moment: Reinventing the Grid for the AI Economy
description:
The data center industry is approaching a historic inflection point. By 2030, global data center power demand is projected to exceed 200 gigawatts, rivaling the electricity consumption of major industrial nations. At the same time, AI workloads are driving rack densities from 20 to 30 kW into the 80 to 150 kW range, with individual campuses scaling into the hundreds of megawatts. The pace of growth is unprecedented. The real challenge is how to power this expansion in a way that strengthens grid reliability, protects ratepayers, and accelerates economic development.

In this keynote, we explore how deeper coordination between data center developers and grid operators is reshaping the energy landscape. From campus-level power innovation and transmission planning to market design and long-term contracting strategies, this discussion will examine how collaboration can reduce volatility, unlock new infrastructure investment, and ensure that AI scale benefits communities rather than burdening them. This is a conversation about leadership, accountability, and building the grid required for the next era of intelligence.
takeaway:

• Why structured partnerships between utilities and data centers can lower long-term electricity costs
• How hyperscale and AI operators are innovating in power architecture and deployment strategy
• What grid operators are doing to manage reliability amid rapid load growth
• How coordinated planning protects both economic development and ratepayer interests

session title: AI Power Block: The Ultimate Solution to AI Data Center Power Bottlenecks
description:
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence since the introduction of large-scale generative models has triggered a profound transformation in global digital infrastructure. As computational intensity accelerates, AI Data Centers (AIDCs) are rapidly emerging as a new infrastructure paradigm—defined by extreme power density, highly dynamic load behavior, and uninterrupted mission-critical operation requirements.

This evolution is fundamentally reshaping the interaction between digital workloads and the power system. Unlike conventional data centers, AI-driven facilities exhibit highly variable and spiky load profiles, characterized by rapid ramp rates, frequent step changes in multi-megawatt demand, and increasingly stringent requirements for power quality, response speed, and system stability at sub-second timescales. These new characteristics are placing unprecedented pressure on existing grid infrastructure and conventional backup architectures, accelerating the need for more adaptive and intelligent energy solutions.



In this keynote, I will examine how these emerging load dynamics are redefining global energy demand patterns and driving a structural shift in grid planning and infrastructure design.

Building on this context, I will introduce the concept of the AI Power Block—an integrated next-generation energy architecture combining advanced power conversion systems (PCS), high-performance battery systems, and intelligent energy management platforms (EMS). This architecture is designed to address the unique operational requirements of AI workloads, including ultra-fast deployment capability, stable performance under highly volatile load conditions, and optimized system-level energy coordination.



Attendees will gain actionable insights into how this solution overcomes grid interconnection barriers, reduces conversion losses, and enables greater renewable integration—ultimately turning energy infrastructure from a passive support function into a grid-interactive, value-generating core asset for the AI economy.
takeaway:
1. Understand why AI workloads are driving unprecedented demands for power availability, grid stability, and compliance with North American grid interconnection rules.

2. Explore how grid-forming battery energy storage systems (BESS) eliminate grid interconnection delays and cut AIDC deployment timelines by enabling faster utility approval.

3. Learn how advanced energy storage solutions smooth volatile AI workloads, enhance voltage ride-through capability, and strengthen overall power resilience for mission-critical operations.

4. Understand how integrated power architectures reduce conversion losses, and support greater renewable energy utilization while lowering operating costs.

5. Gain practical, field-proven insights into deploying grid-forming energy storage solutions that deliver scalable power, and support sustainable AIDC operations in ERCOT and other North American markets.

description: As AI-driven load growth strains grid infrastructure across every major market, wholesale power costs are becoming one of the most consequential financial variables in data center project economics. Getting the hedge structure right depends heavily on a data center's specific use case and utilization profile, and what works for one operator can leave another significantly exposed. session title: State of Data Center Power 2026: How the Ecosystem Is Changing and Where It's Headed
description: The data center and energy industries are converging as AI workloads drive unprecedented density and capacity demands that challenge traditional power planning models. Bill Kleyman, provides a comprehensive industry overview of where the data center power ecosystem stands today and where it's headed, drawing on the latest AFCOM research and market developments. The session examines which power strategies are working in today's market, where challenges remain, and how approaches differ by geography and scale, covering behind-the-meter generation, battery storage, microgrids, utility partnerships, and regulatory engagement. Operators will gain practical insights for evaluating emerging solutions and developing power roadmaps that balance availability, cost, sustainability, and operational flexibility.
speakers: Bill Kleyman(Apolo.us)

session title: Bridging the Energy Gap: A C-Suite Survey of Critical Problems and Real-World Answers
description: Data center designers, builders, owners, and operators are facing constant pressure to meet ever-increasing, and often extremely public, gaps in energy. These gaps range from addressing the microsecond bursts associated with AI workloads, to the typical seconds-to-minutes of power quality and short-duration energy transfers, all the way to the years needed to acquire access to new electricity sources, despite stranded or cyclical capacity that's available under the right scenarios. This wide-ranging C-suite panel discussion brings together industry leaders to explore trends, resources, and innovative solutions to these challenges. Topics include cogeneration, waste heat recovery, reducing peak PUE, improving end-to-end efficiency from high voltage to DC, co-generation and self-generation strategies, and planning day-ahead for increased capacity, including opportunities to tap into low-cost or even free electricity. The focus lands firmly on real-world scenarios being deployed today, revealing how leading operators are turning energy constraints into competitive advantages through smarter planning, innovative technologies, and creative use of existing grid resources.
speakers: David Tearse(Karman Industries), Sai Shivareddy(Nyobolt), Astrid Atkinson(Camus Energy), Jack Pouchet(Pouchet Advisory Services, LLC), Yang Liu(Electric Hydrogen), Greg Andrews(S+S Industries)

session title: Co-Building the Future: Partnerships Between Data Centers and Energy Developers
description: Power is now the primary bottleneck to digital infrastructure growth. In this panel discussion, data center developers and energy leaders will confront the realities of delivering power and energy at the scale, speed, and sustainability required by these workloads. Panelists will review whether current models, grid connection, PPA, on-site generation, renewable integration, are sufficient, and what new approaches are needed. The conversation will highlight collaboration strategies, risk-sharing mechanisms, and how to accelerate time-to-power in an increasingly constrained energy landscape. Expect a forward-looking discussion on co-development and the evolving role of energy partners in data center expansion. Attendees will gain practical insights into emerging partnership models, strategies for navigating regulatory and grid constraints, and actionable approaches to de-risking power delivery timelines
speakers: Ana Quelhas(EDP), Daniel Droog(Chevron New Energies), Elaine Walsh(Baker Botts)

session title: Demand Response and Virtual Power Plants: How Data Centers Become Electric Grid Assets
description:
Data centers looking to power new facilities face a perfect storm: interconnection queues stretching years, surging energy costs, and growing community scrutiny over power consumption. The rise of demand response, distributed energy resource, and virtual power plant platforms is helping data centers overcome each of those obstacles. Data center operators are using on-site battery storage, backup generation, and flexible workloads to shift from passive energy consumers into active grid participants.

This session explores how hyperscalers, colocation providers, and enterprise data centers can apply these strategies and platforms to shorten interconnection timelines, reduce operating costs, and generate new cash flows while maintaining uptime. It will also explain how the emerging Bring Your Own Capacity (BYOC) model lets developers bring virtual power plant capacity to utilities to fast-track grid access.

Attendees will learn how grid participation can help data centers gain community and regulator support by reducing peak demand, supporting reliability, and deferring new infrastructure investments. The session will demonstrate how operators can unlock new revenue streams from assets they already own, cut years off interconnection timelines, and strategically flex workloads during grid events and market opportunities. Participants will also gain a practical framework for evaluating demand response opportunities that align with their operational requirements and business objectives.
speakers: Adam Scarsella(Voltus), Nate Soles(CPower)

session title: Designing for Density: Supporting Enterprise AI Workloads Without Overbuilding Infrastructure
description: The data center industry has been concentrated in a small number of major markets, but power constraints, cooling limits, and land availability can limit development in traditional hubs while enterprise demand keeps growing. This session examines the opportunity for data center expansion in regional and underserved markets, highlighting what operators and enterprise customers are seeing in successful deployments in Ohio, South Carolina, and other markets. As a data center operator and developer, DartPoints will share how it has brought capacity online in these environments, how it balances speed-to-market with long-term scalability, what has surprised them, and what they would approach differently today.
speakers: Scott Willis(DartPoints)

session title: Nuclear Renaissance: How and When Fission, Fusion, and Hybrid Technologies Can Change the Data Center Power Stack
description:
There's no way that all the proposed projects in this epoch-defining data center buildout can come true using the existing power infrastructure. Enter a new role for nuclear power — traditional fission, small modular reactors (SMRs), fusion, and hybrid models, with their promise to provide abundant, low-emission baseload power. With these models, the future of nuclear power generation technology looks much different than what has defined the nuclear industry to date.

In this session, an expert panel will explore:



	*
Scientific models and timelines for fission, fusion, and hybrid models

	*
Explanations of the different models including traditional fission, SMR, magnetic fusion, fission-fusion hybrid

	*
Regulatory, legal, and investment scenarios to reduce time to scale

	*
Variations in nuclear investment across geographies

	*
Hyperscaler investment in nuclear technologies

	*
Where nuclear technologies fit in the broader data center 'energy stack'
speakers: Romi Mahajan(ExoFusion), Stuart Allen(FusionX), Amy Roma(Orrick), Matthias Knolker(General Atomics Magnetic Fusion Energy), Patrick Ellis(Type One Energy)

session title: Beyond Power Density: How AI Is Reshaping Data Center Infrastructure Design
description:
The rapid growth of AI workloads is fundamentally changing how data centers are designed and operated. While early discussions focused primarily on rack power density, the industry is now facing a broader infrastructure transformation. Liquid cooling is becoming the default for high-density AI deployments, and deterministic high-performance networking is emerging as a co-equal constraint alongside power and cooling. At the same time, AI infrastructure is bifurcating between centralized training clusters and distributed inference deployments across metro regions.

This session will explore how AI workloads are reshaping data center power delivery, cooling architecture, and network design, and what operators, engineers, and infrastructure planners should expect over the next three to five years. We will discuss rack density trends, liquid cooling operational boundaries, east-west network traffic growth driven by AI inference and agentic workloads, and how these trends are changing facility design, interconnection strategy, and operational responsibilities.

Key takeaways will include:



• Considerations about workload placement beyond power availability, including ecosystem proximity, interconnection, and data locality
• A practical lens for evaluating how AI workload type (training vs. inference) drives fundamentally different infrastructure design decisions

	* A clear understanding of liquid cooling today and how to think about facility upgrades sequencing

	* Perspective on why network architecture is becoming a first-order infrastructure constraint, and how observability across the network is key to optimized AI workload performance and economics, not just a connectivity layer
speakers: Kyle Chien(Digital Realty), Vinod Kamath(Lenovo)

session title: Evaluating Data Center Power Architectures Against Emerging Grid Oscillation Standards for AI Workloads
description: As AI workloads drive unprecedented demand, utilities and grid operators have published measurable standards defining allowable load oscillation limits at the point of interconnection. This session examines how modern data center power architectures can meet emerging grid requirements, comparing AC, hybrid, DC, and storage-assisted approaches against forced oscillation limits and ramp rate constraints. Drawing on perspectives from GPU manufacturers, power system OEMs, and data center operators, the discussion moves from GPU load profiles at the rack level through how power distribution architectures must respond, and ultimately, which design choices enable compliance without compromising performance as AI deployments scale.
speakers: David Roop(Mitsubishi Electric Power Products, Inc.), John Campion(Mitsubishi Electric Power Products, Inc.), Rajesh Gopinath(Oracle), Sai Somayajula(Nvidia)

session title: Who Owns the Power Problem Now? Rethinking Grid Reliance, On‑Site Power, and Risk Allocation
description:
As AI‑driven load growth accelerates, data center power strategy is shifting from a single‑counterparty utility model to a more active, multi‑layered approach that blends grid collaboration, on‑site and behind‑the‑meter solutions, storage, and emerging clean firm power. These changes are forcing operators, hyperscalers, utilities, and capital providers to rethink who owns which risks, and how those risks are priced.
This roundtable will bring together perspectives from across the data center power ecosystem to discuss how power procurement, control, and financing strategies are evolving in response to interconnection delays, power density constraints, regulatory uncertainty, and resilience expectations. Participants will explore what is working in practice today, where models are breaking down, and how both operators and investors are evaluating critical approaches such as co‑located generation, microgrids, and alternative contracting structures.
speakers: Rachel Rosenfeld(Norton Rose Fulbright US LLP), Erin McPike(FTI Consulting, Strategic Communications), Lavinia Macovschi(ING Bank N.V.)

session title: Wind, Solar, and Storage: What the Future Holds for This Renewable Power Trifecta
description: Wind and solar power generation initiatives for data centers are increasingly treated as hybrid systems that bundle generation with long duration energy storage. More efficient storage makes it practical to produce energy when the sun's shining and wind blowing and let data centers access it when they need it. This panel will explore where wind-solar-storage systems fit in the data center energy stack, especially as pressure rises for data centers to provide more of their own power.
speakers: Mike Sloan(Synergetic LLC), Ian Rock(TerraFlow Energy)

session title: 800V and Beyond: Solid-State Transformers as the Foundation of AI Data Center Infrastructure
description: As AI workloads push rack power densities toward 600kW and beyond, the multi-stage conversion architectures that have defined data center power delivery for decades are reaching their physical and economic limits. Solid-state transformers, enabling direct medium-voltage AC to 800V DC conversion in a single step, are emerging as the power delivery architecture purpose-built for next-generation AI infrastructure. Drawing on utility and hyperscale deployments already in production, this session examines what the shift to solid-state means for how developers and operators design, build, and scale data center power infrastructure over the next five to ten years, and what those evaluating their next build or retrofit need to understand about where this technology fits today.
speakers: Jake Ring(Power and Data Management LLC)

session title: AI-Native Energy Intelligence: From Reactive Management to Continuous Optimization in Data Center Operations
description: Data center operators face growing pressure to reduce energy costs while maintaining uptime and performance, but many energy management approaches still stop at monitoring and reactive decision-making. Moving from reactive response to continuous predictive optimization requires a new methodology, one where AI-native energy intelligence enables closed-loop control across complex power and cooling infrastructure. Operator case studies will demonstrate how this approach reduces energy consumption, carbon emissions, operating costs, and equipment wear while improving reliability and operational resilience. Attendees will understand why the next step in data center energy management is not simply better monitoring, but intelligent systems that continuously identify, validate, and improve performance as a real control layer for modern operations.
speakers: Niklas Panten(etalytics Inc)

session title: Geothermal Rising: How New Technology Has Changed Its Place in the Power Stack
description: Geothermal has long been treated as a niche power source, limited by geography and overshadowed by the scale of wind and solar. A convergence of technologies, advanced drilling techniques, subsurface engineering, reservoir stimulation, and real-time sensing and modeling, is changing its role in the power stack entirely, unlocking heat resources in regions where conventional geothermal was never commercially viable. The result is firm, around-the-clock power that can now be procured in markets that were previously out of reach, and major hyperscalers are already signing long-term PPAs to take advantage of it. This session examines enhanced geothermal as a practical power procurement decision data center operators can make today, covering where the technology is currently deployable, what the procurement process looks like, and why the geographic reach of next-generation geothermal is fundamentally different from anything the industry has had access to before.
speakers: Lucy Darago(XGS Energy), Dawn Owens(Fervo Energy), Alan Howard(Omdia (Informa TechTarget))

session title: When Backup Becomes Baseload: Operating Onsite Power Reliably
description: Data center power teams are under pressure to secure new generation, but installed megawatts are not the same as dependable megawatts. As onsite gas turbines and reciprocating engines shift from backup assets to baseload or frequent-use power sources, operational readiness becomes as critical as procurement. This session will explore how teams can use operating data, failure probability, and cost consequence to understand how much onsite generation capacity they can actually count on—and what it takes to operate that capacity reliably under mission-critical conditions. Drawing on decades of experience across gas turbines and power systems, the discussion will address maintenance strategy, fleet health monitoring, dispatch decisions, and the operational tradeoffs that emerge when backup becomes baseload. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for translating installed capacity into dependable capacity and building a resilient onsite power strategy.
speakers: Corson Teasley(Turbine Logic)

session title: Where Should AI Agents Fit In Data Center Critical Infrastructure Decisions?
description: In the age of agentic AI, building autonomous systems is getting fast and cheap. The most critical work involves the judgment about what to deploy, what to integrate, what to ignore, and who takes responsibility for the decisions made. In and around the data center power room, those are fundamental operational choices. AI-powered systems are playing a growing role in data centers, landing in commissioning, building management systems, demand response, energy procurement, and electrical asset management. if an agent dispatches incorrectly or overcommits load on a 200 MW campus, somebody has to answer, to the regulator, the insurer, the board. This session offers the operator's perspective on deploying production agentic AI in power-intensive, regulated, critical-infrastructure environments, covering what accountability architecture actually looks like for agents in the power stack, how operators are partitioning autonomous, assisted, and human-only decisions, and why, as the technology layer commoditizes, the judgment layer is becoming the entire premium.
speakers: Vova Soroka(Apolo Cloud)

session title: KEYNOTE: Agile Infrastructure for AI: Holistic Data Center Co-Design from Chip to Utility
description:
AI infrastructure is growing at an unprecedented pace, with Google now processing more than 3 quadrillion tokens per month, representing a 7x year-over-year increase in compute demand from May 2025 to May 2026. Meeting this velocity requires new innovations in energy efficiency and power delivery. Tom Garvens, Vice President of Data Center Technology and Systems at Google, presents a keynote demonstrating how Google is addressing this scale responsibly through a full-stack approach that ensures data centers act as proactive, stabilizing partners to local grids.

To address the critical speed mismatch between rapid AI rollout and multi-year utility grid expansion, Google is engineering infrastructure for extreme agility. Key to this approach are dynamic energy strategies—such as transforming clean backup assets into primary grid-support, tools during peak demand, intelligent load shaping, and power load smoothing techniques — that prevent disruptive power swings and actively support utility resilience.

Beyond these dynamic energy strategies, Google is co-designing holistic solutions spanning from chip to utility — optimizing for liquid cooling, Low Voltage Direct Current (LVDC) architectures, intelligent algorithms and data center facility design. A core pillar of this work is open ecosystem innovation: publishing standardized power and facility technology specifications through communities like OCP so the entire industry can build interoperable, efficient, and sustainable infrastructure.
speakers: Tom Garvens(Google)

description: This session on nuclear integration with data centers will cover demand outlooks, new nuclear construction, and key considerations for colocating nuclear generation with data center infrastructure. Led by two nuclear industry experts, it will address practical challenges such as AI-driven load variability and power quality impacts on nuclear power plants, along with topics including behind-the-meter electrical integration, nuclear-integrated cooling concepts, and the role of thermal energy storage in combined nuclear–data center systems. It will wrap up with a forward-looking, open dialogue on the enablers and obstacles to the future of nuclear–data center integration.

session title: Community Pushback: How Data Centers and Utilities Can Address Power Concerns and Earn Support
description: Building community support for data center projects requires early engagement, deliberate relationship-building, and a willingness to address the power-specific concerns that communities have around electricity rates, power reliability, and the environment. Operators and developers need to address such concerns early and consistently to get projects approved. Calvert Street Group, which brings two decades of public affairs and coalition-building experience to the data center approval process, will bring together stakeholders in this process to explore how productive community dialogue can build durable local support before concerns harden into organized opposition.
speakers: Rajiv Vohra(Thor Equities), Diane Sullivan(Hecate Energy LLC), Matt Bailey(Calvert Street Group)

session title: Control Systems for Data Center Microgrids: Turning Compliance into Reliability and Revenue
description: As data centers invest in more on-site generation and storage to supplement to meet power needs, their relationship with the electrical grid is fundamentally changing, including the regulatory expectations. NERC is moving to require data centers to register as Computational Load Entities due to the size of their power requirements, with mandatory reliability standards covering curtailment, islanding, and voltage ride-though expected to follow. Non-compliance could mean forced curtailments, interconnection delays, or operational restrictions that hit uptime and revenue. This session will explore how the IEEE 2030.7 microgrid control standard provides a practical framework for managing behind-the-meter systems while meeting obligations such as these, including modeling and optimization tools that show how operators can turn compliance requirements into improved reliability and even revenue opportunities.
speakers: Jim Reilly(Reilly Associates), Michael Stadler(Xendee Corporation)

session title: From Queue to Megawatts: A Realistic Playbook for Deliverable Power in the AI Era
description: The pipeline of proposed U.S. data center projects has surged to 780 GW, which for comparison would be larger than the largest recorded U.S. peak load capacity. While it's understood that more than half of that is speculative and likely won't get built anytime soon, it's nevertheless true that the gap between hoped-for megawatts and realistically deliverable megawatts is widening at a pace that makes even seasoned planners blink. This session, presented from a data center operator and developer perspective, offers a pragmatic, technically grounded playbook for what is actually buildable, examining interconnection queue realities and the due diligence signals that separate viable sites from speculative ones. It will also look at factors that suggest whether behind-the-meter proposals are genuine solutions versus paper megawatts.
speakers: Sarah Spencer-Workman(NTT Global)

session title: BESS Best Practices: Optimizing Battery Energy Storage Systems in Their Increasingly Critical Role
description: As battery energy storage systems move from backup afterthought to core infrastructure in data center power strategy, the operational decisions that determine whether they perform as expected are becoming as consequential as the procurement decisions that put them in the ground. This session brings together two distinct perspectives on what it actually takes to run BESS effectively at data center scale, covering the deployment and integration side, including how battery systems get financed, sited, and coordinated with onsite generation and utility partners to accelerate interconnection, and the software and controls side, covering how intelligent dispatch, real-time asset health monitoring, and multi-mode optimization determine whether a deployed system delivers its full value or leaves performance on the table. Operators leave with a practical framework for evaluating both stages of the BESS lifecycle, from the strategic and engineering decisions made before commissioning to the operational choices that determine performance across the asset's lifetime.
speakers: Pasi Taimela(FlexGen), Phil Martin(Calibrant Energy)

session title: How ERCOT's Unique Market Structure Shapes Power Procurement Strategies for Texas Data Centers
description: Texas' unique ERCOT energy-only market structure is creating both challenges and opportunities for data center power procurement, driven by rapid system and market transformation that is reshaping how operators and developers approach behind-the-meter generation, microgrid development, and contracting strategies. This discussion will bring together developers, operators, regulators, and capital providers to examine how evolving regulatory dynamics and interconnection processes directly influence power decisions in Texas, with practical insights into structuring BTM assets, mitigating curtailment risk, and positioning projects for long-term scalability in one of the most active and rapidly changing grid environments in the country.
speakers: Meghan Griffiths(Jackson Walker), Shaun Connell(Lancium)

session title: Operating at Gigawatt Scale: Real-World Lessons Learned and Opportunities Ahead
description: Few organizations have crossed the 1 GW operational threshold, and scaling data center infrastructure to that level across a distributed portfolio requires confronting power infrastructure challenges that simply don't exist at smaller scale. From transmission interconnections and dynamic load management to the operational demands of direct-to-chip and immersion liquid cooling at extreme rack densities, the complexity compounds quickly. Drawing on direct hyperscale experience, this session shares practical strategies for building resilient gigawatt-scale operations, including AI-driven predictive maintenance, real-time power-workload orchestration, and frameworks for early utility engagement, giving infrastructure professionals a clearer picture of what they are actually building toward.
speakers: Jose Rodriguez(New Era Energy & Digital, Inc.), Aaron Tasin(2G Energy North America)

session title: Emerging Battery Technologies: Comparing the Next Generation of Batteries for Data Center Deployment
description: As energy storage becomes a core element of data center power strategy operators are expanding their evaluation criteria to understand what better fit their specific use cases, whether that means improved safety profiles, longer duration performance, supply chain diversity, or different cost structures over a facility's lifetime. This session brings together representatives from several battery chemistries to discuss the distinct performance characteristics, deployment considerations, and real-world tradeoffs of each as it applies to data center power needs. The goal is to give end users a clearer framework for evaluating which storage technology fits which problem, so that the next storage investment decision is made with a full picture of what the market currently offers beyond familiar defaults.
speakers: Daniel Sottosanti(XL Batteries), Brandon Smith(ZincFive), Paul Durkee(Peak Energy), Mark Thompson(Form Energy)

session title: Spark Session: Three Emerging Innovators Challenging Data Centers' Power and Cooling Status Quo
description: As data centers face mounting pressure over water consumption, thermal waste, and the carbon intensity of their power supply, a new wave of technologies is emerging that treats these liabilities as solvable engineering problems rather than unavoidable trade-offs. Shumate Engineering makes the case for a hybrid adiabatic cooling approach that dramatically reduces both water use and power consumption without sacrificing performance. Atoco presents an atmospheric water harvesting system powered by Nobel Prize-winning materials science that converts data center waste heat into clean water. Apollo Investments introduces Advanced Hybrid Distributed Energy Resources (AHDER), a distributed energy system designed to generate power from conventional fuels while capturing rather than emitting carbon. Data Center World Power's Spark Session format brings together emerging technologies in a rapid-fire, back-to-back presentation style designed to challenge assumptions and spark innovation.
speakers: Justin Penrod(Shumate Engineering), Magnus Bach(Atoco, Inc.), Wen Li(Apollo Investments, LLC)

session title: Speed to Power: A Practical Roadmap for Compressing Data Center Power Timelines
description: Data center operators and developers want power in months, not years, and grid-based delivery timelines aren't closing that gap on their own. Drawing on direct experience advising utilities, behind-the-meter developers, and large-load data center customers, this panel discussion walks through the specific program management, procurement, and utility engagement decisions that help compress timelines. The discussion will cover tough topics such as the long-lead equipment contracting choices that can protect or destroy schedules and the organizational capabilities that help separate operators that deliver power on time from those that don't.
speakers: Evan Fairmont(FMI Corp), Blake Angelo(FMI Corp)

session title: The Brownfield Advantage: How to Scale Existing Data Centers for Bigger Power and Cooling Performance
description: With increasing AI and high-performance workloads, data centers are constantly being pushed to higher levels of power density, scalability and cooling performance, putting pressure on operators to speed up deployment timelines while still meeting local and regulatory requirements. This session will share how scaling for extreme density doesn't always require building from the ground up, with brownfield sites, where power, cooling, and connectivity already exists, often offer a faster and more efficient approach. It will also look at how these sites can be adapted to support greater thermal loads, including ways to manage heat more efficiently, with practical examples of how to approach scalability, high-density deployments, and cooling challenges in ways that balances speed, performance, sustainability, and reliability.
speakers: Monica Brisimitzakis(Patmos)
